extracted.intended_audience: new and beginning school teachers (primary/elementary; small schools)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for teachers beginning a new school: how to observe pupils, establish order, arrange seating and classes, and handle misconduct in the first days and weeks. Emphasizes cautions, conversational discipline, and protecting pupils' character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and observe existing routines at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to remodel the school wholly at once; learn the usual order of exercises and, at first, employ the same routines and assignments that were in place under the former teacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain a memorandum of the usual order of exercises (examples: ask pupils what lessons were first heard, which recited together, etc.), set pupils at work preparing for next-day lessons, and use private conversation to supplement this knowledge. The text: 'it is not probable that he would long continue these arrangements unaltered... the teacher, in hearing the different classes, would watch for opportunities for combining them...'; treat the initial period as a time to get everything 'under sail' before steering changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make early, careful observation to learn pupils' characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first days to discover who are idle, mischievous, docile, or likely to be troublesome; identify those who will require special watch and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid immediate harsh measures so you can 'obtain time for observation' and note tendencies (they often sit in knots). Note names of the most prominent troublemakers and inquire out of school about their characters and home education. The author cautions that some teachers even let pupils have near-full freedom for a few days to reveal characters, though that may go too far.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty or public punishment in the opening days
rubrics_metrics.description: Postpone severe or public measures until you are acquainted with a pupil's general character; rash action at the outset often injures both pupil and teacher influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: do not call out and shame a boy for a single petty act on day one (apple incident). Use a mild, under-tone rebuke if necessary, and reserve hard measures until you know whether the offense is habitual. 'It would be safer to postpone such decided measures a little' is explicit advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment based on appearance; trust conduct, not manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not form unfavorable opinions of pupils from their air, bearing, or tone alone; wait for 'the most sure and unequivocal evidences of character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners are prone to prejudge on looks. The teacher should 'suspend his judgment' and remember that many docile and faithful pupils may first appear unattractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond proportionately to minor misconduct; avoid anger and excessive reproach
rubrics_metrics.description: Many school offences are momentary expressions of childhood; treat them as inconveniences to be repressed, not as heinous sins deserving severe punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a tone and manner that indicate you understand the moral character of the act; restrain irregularities but do so without displaying anger or impatience. This preserves moral perspective and teacher authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate types of misconduct and tailor treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a broad distinction between momentary thoughtlessness and real moral turpitude (wilful mischief, habitual disobedience, open rebellion), and treat each category differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve sterner measures for genuine, intentional wrongdoing. The teacher 'should show that he distinguishes these cases from such momentary acts of thoughtlessness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate pupils whose companionship tempts misbehavior, but do so cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more pupils together tend to play or corrupt one another, seat them apart; however, do this only after careful observation and with tact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the school early for undesirable groupings; avoid immediate separation based on first impressions. If you must move seats, do it 'cautiously, deliberately, and with good nature' and keep the motive out of view to prevent injury to reputation or resentment. The text gives guidance on waiting until you know 'actual character' before making changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use frank, conversational engagement and probation before punitive separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak kindly and frankly with pupils about seating or conduct, offer choices or a trial period to reform (probation), and monitor before enforcing separation or punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example dialogue: let two friends choose to remain together on condition of 'extra exertion' and tell them you 'shall soon see' — if they fail, you can separate them later without resentment. This approach stimulates responsibility and reduces need for immediate harsh action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ private post-school conferences and measured suspense to elicit honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: When misconduct repeats, request pupils to wait after school for a private talk; the interval helps reflection and makes a candid admission more likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let them stand a few minutes in expectation if appropriate; ask open, non-accusatory questions and resist immediate punishment. Example scenes show the teacher asking 'What do you think I ought to do next?' and eliciting voluntary commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront active troublemakers openly but with good humor and kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: For pupils who intentionally seek to make difficulty, it is often best to face them directly while maintaining good humor, frankness, and personal kindness to de-escalate and reclaim them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: the lath-and-string prank — teacher pretends not to know, lets guilty boy remove the string, then discusses the matter privately while protecting his reputation; the club example — teacher sits beside the boy, talks kindly, and persuades him to throw the club away. These methods rely on surprise, friendliness, and appeal to better feelings rather than threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect pupils' reputations; avoid public exposure unless carefully justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publicly exposing or ridiculing pupils; public disgrace often does lasting harm to character and can produce sullen or reckless responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must make the offence public, conceal the offender's name where possible (lath example). Let the school condemn the action without making one child the object of universal shame. 'Every exertion should be made... to avoid, at the beginning, every unnecessary sacrifice' of reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public exposure/shame selectively when it will reform and you command majority sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare cases (e.g., a large, self-conceited boy abusing smaller ones), public exposure and mild humiliation can check bad influence and humble pride — but only if the offender's character and the school climate make it likely to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the exposure is mild, avoids harsh exaggeration, secures the sympathies of other pupils, and is adapted to 'work well as a remedy.' Example: the Richard Jones sled case, where the teacher frames a moral lesson for the class and leads them to condemn the behaviour without cruel language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate background and gather information before decisive discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Make inquiries out of school about pupils who appear most likely to cause trouble — learn about home character and previous history — before employing decisive disciplinary measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends noting the most prominent troublesome pupils and 'make inquiries out of school respecting them,—their characters,—their education at home, &c.' This background informs proportionate and effective responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust class groupings and recitation times over time to fit your plan
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial observation, watch for opportunities to combine classes, discontinue small ones, alter recitation times, and regroup scholars so the school's organization better matches the teacher's views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These changes should be gradual and practical: 'a school is like a ship... most easily steered in the right direction, when under sail.' The author notes that detailed individual positioning is feasible in moderate-size schools but that larger schools may require more summary processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with circumspection, patience, frankness, and good will
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the school government through mild, steady authority based on patient observation, frankness, and honest good will toward every pupil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concluding guidance: by commencing with these virtues the teacher 'will find less difficulty at the outset' and 'soon have the satisfaction of perceiving that a mild but most efficient government is quietly and firmly established.' This is a summary principle that underlies the other specific measures.
